claim: A rotary's slow rate byte indexes the same printed table every other rate byte on this unit indexes -- the wide one, picked by the `0.05 - 10.0` the page prints against it, with no constant of its own anywhere in it. What the rotary adds is that the entry is where a rotor is sent and not where it ends up. Sent down, it arrives exactly -- which is measured and not inferred: the same byte written after a faster one, with no reset between, comes back on its entry where the same byte written after a reset comes back short of it. Sent up, it stops a fixed distance short: 0.245 Hz on the low rotor and 0.062 on the high, holding to a thousandth of a hertz from the corner to the top of the byte and across both places the table's own step changes. And where the distance to the entry is narrower than that, the rotor barely sets off, so five entries of the low rotor's table return one rate and the high rotor moves a fifth of an entry across the one entry of its own. The width of that flat stretch and the size of the gap are the same number, which is what separates this from a constant subtracted after a lookup: read the gap off the top of the sweep alone and it places the corner, which neither half of the fit was shown. The distance is set by the acceleration byte the page prints against each rotor, and the two rotors are one routine reached twice: at every one of nine settings of that byte the two gaps agree to a median of 2.8 per cent, so the four to one between them is the two defaults and not the two rotors. What that byte does is a claim of its own beside this one.
named: a first-order lag done with an arithmetic right shift, which underflows climbing and floors falling
adds: The records say what frequency each take's partials agreed the modulator ran at, at each setting of one byte, with the other rotor's Level byte named in the held block. What is read out of them here is that the byte indexes the closed table, that the entry is a target rather than a rate, that the arrival is one-sided, and that the two rotors' gaps are a power of two apart. The records name no table, no arrival and no acceleration, and each says in its own limits that a type with more than one modulator returns whichever dominates it.
refutedBy: A rotor sent down to an entry arriving short of it as well, which would make the gap a property of the table rather than of the arrival. Or the flat stretch at the bottom of the byte turning out to be a different width from the gap, which would make them two numbers rather than one. Or the acceleration byte turning out not to move the gap at all, which would leave the gap unexplained and the reading a description rather than a mechanism.

eraPriors.claim: A rotor's speed is closed towards its target by `x += (target - x) >> k`, which is a subtract, an arithmetic shift and an add, and no multiply or divide anywhere.
eraPriors.why: It is the cheapest lag a control processor of this period can run, `k` is a small integer, and `0 - 15` is exactly the four bits a shift count fits in -- which is what the page prints against each rotor's acceleration.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The gap were symmetric. That loop's defect is one-sided: climbing, the shift underflows to nothing while the difference is still about two to the k wide and the loop stops there; falling, an arithmetic shift of a negative number floors rather than rounding towards zero, so the last step is always taken and the target is reached. Both halves were measured. Every entry under where the rotor rests is returned exactly, on both rotors, and every entry above it is returned short.

eraPriors.claim: The two rotors are not one routine with one constant: a drum has more mass than a horn, so their accelerations default apart, and if the lag is a shift then apart means by a whole power of two.
eraPriors.why: It is what the effect is a model of, and it is why the page prints two acceleration parameters rather than one.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The two gaps had stood in a ratio that is not near a power of two. They stand at 3.952 to one.

alternatives.reading: The distance a rotor stops short by is set by its printed acceleration, and being a shift count it changes by whole factors of two rather than smoothly.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Half of it, and the half this claim leant on is the half that fell. The byte does set the distance -- it moves it over a factor of 335 across its range -- and it is read through its top four bits, which five boundary pairs say. But the entries are not a shift count doubling per step: over the first ten of them the distance is one constant divided by the entry's position plus one, which is a multiply before the shift and not the shift. So the four to one between the two rotors' defaults is where those two defaults sit in that table, and reading it as two powers of two was reading a coincidence. The byte has its own claim beside this one, and this claim's sentence about it has been taken out.

alternatives.reading: Where a rotor rests when the type is switched on is a state it is put into, not a rate it was left at -- so a byte written twice without a reset between would be answered from wherever the first write left the rotor.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It was asked. The rotor keeps its speed between writes: the byte written down to setting 32 from setting 127, with no reset between, reads 1.652 Hz on the low rotor against 1.4071 for the same byte after a reset -- 0.2315 octaves apart, where the model says 0.2319. On the high rotor the two are 0.0546 apart against a model saying 0.0553. The other half of the run is the control it needs: a rotor climbing to the top of the table from an entry it had already reached stops where one climbing from rest stops, to six hundred-thousandths of an octave on the low rotor -- so the gap is a property of the step and not of how far the rotor travelled, which is the one thing a lag caught in flight could not say.

alternatives.reading: The gap is a property of the take rather than of the rotor: ten seconds of settling was not enough and every reading is of a rotor still closing.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: What the gap does with the distance the rotor had to travel. A lag caught mid-flight leaves a gap in proportion to the one it set out with, so the gap would grow across the sweep; it holds instead, to a thousandth of a hertz from setting 16 to 127. Scored through the class's own gates that reading is 0.07489 octaves against the winner's 0.00092 on the low rotor and it leans on every record of both rotors. The record that did not record its settled time is the one that shows what a rotor still closing looks like: its gap runs from 0.2425 Hz at setting 32 to 0.3306 at 127, where the settled run's holds.

alternatives.reading: A constant number of hertz is taken off every entry, with nothing to do with where the rotor was.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The bottom of the table, which is what the sixty second takes were made to reach. The low rotor's gap is 0.2447 Hz and its first entry is 0.05, so this reading has the rotor turning backwards there; the unit returns 0.0497, and the reading is 5.64559 octaves out at its worst. It is refuted a second time by a record it was never scored against: the low rotor left at its own default of 6 reads 0.35 Hz across twenty-one takes of three other bytes, and this reading says 0.105.

alternatives.reading: The rotary reads the shared table through a multiplier, so what looks like a constant taken off is a ratio.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: That the gap does not grow. A multiplier is a straight line through the origin and the readings are a straight line that misses it, so the best multiplier is 0.8972 and it is 0.15823 octaves out in the middle and leaning on every record of both rotors.

alternatives.reading: The arrival is short by a fixed time rather than by a fixed rate -- a rotor that takes a few milliseconds longer per turn than it was asked to.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The top of the range, which the eight second records reach and the sixty second ones do not. A fixed time is a shrinking number of hertz as the rotor speeds up, so a period long enough to explain the gap at 1.65 Hz explains almost none of it at 10, and this reading is 1.41316 octaves out on the record it was not fitted to -- more than an octave, on readings four partials agree on to a thousandth of a hertz.

gates.name: gross
gates.why: A median of 0.00092 and 0.00071 octaves on the two sixty second records, against spans of 2.4898 and 5.0014 octaves that these bytes command. The worst point on either is at a setting where the closed table itself is off by the same amount on both rotors -- entry 8 reads 0.4481 and 0.4482 where the table says 0.45, and another type's slot reads 0.4485 there -- so it is the table's own rounding and not the rotary's.

gates.name: properties
gates.why: Three, and none of them is the residual. The arrival is one-sided: every entry under where the rotor rests is returned exactly and every entry above it short, on both rotors. The width of the flat stretch is the size of the gap: read the gap off the settings from 21 up, where nothing about the corner is visible, and read where the rotor rests off the settings to 15, where nothing has moved, and the settings between -- which neither half was shown -- come back within 0.0019 octaves on the low rotor and 0.0021 on the high apart from the one point named above. And the two gaps stand at 3.952 to one, which is a power of two on a part whose page prints a four-bit acceleration per rotor.

gates.name: power
gates.why: Five other readings were scored on all five records and every one of them leans on the record it was fitted to. Each fails where its own structure lives and nowhere else: the constant subtraction takes the first entries of the table past nothing, the multiplier has to make the gap grow, the lag caught mid-flight has to make it grow in proportion to the distance travelled, the arrival read on the period has to make it shrink towards the top, and the table read plain has no corner at all. The strongest of them is the table read plain, which is the closed claim's own model unaltered rather than a copy written for this comparison -- and it is out by 0.49124 octaves at the corner.

gates.name: breakdown
gates.why: No record of either rotor comes back structured, and the signed median swings less than the floor of one table entry on every one of the five.

figures.read_as: The one point of daylight is the high rotor at setting 16, where the rotor moved 0.0135 Hz and this reading says it should not have moved at all. reproduces.how_the_model_is_read: Through the rate class's own scorer, in octaves, against the coarser of what the run resolved from its partials' disagreement and what one entry of the table is worth -- which on these records is the entry, by two orders. The table is the closed claim's and is copied into every candidate unaltered, so what is being scored is what each says the rotor does with the entry and nothing else. Two parameters per rotor are fitted, on the sixty second record alone, by one fine grid with no coarse pass; the eight second records are then answered untouched.

what_the_fit_could_not_choose.what: Where the rotor rests is pinned by a handful of settings and by nothing else in the sweep, so the median is flat across a stretch of it and picks a point inside that stretch rather than the point.
what_the_fit_could_not_choose.read_as: On the low rotor the two readings agree, because five settings sit on the flat stretch. On the high rotor one does, and the median's answer and the direct one are 0.0135 Hz apart -- which is the whole of the model's worst point on that record. Reading it off the setting the rotor was aimed above and did not move from removes that point and costs a ten-thousandth of an octave of median, so the record does not choose between them and the published figure is the median's.

and_at_a_setting_neither_sweep_asked.read_as: Two halves of the arrival, each tested where the other cannot reach. Neither setting was asked by either sweep, neither record was fitted on, and what picks them out is the byte the unit was measured to power the type up holding rather than anything chosen here.

reproduces.and_where_the_verdict_holds: From value 16 up, which is where the comparison is made. Below it the reading is withdrawn: the readings stand as readings and the model still returns them, but a second record of the same byte on the same type returns something else, so neither is a reading of the byte alone. What took the bottom away is in `what_the_write_timing_took`.

and_when_the_byte_was_written_twice.what: The two records the claim's second alternative queued, scored through the same gates with nothing refitted. Each carries four takes: one byte written after a reset and the same byte written after the other end of the range, both ways round.
and_when_the_byte_was_written_twice.why_the_floor_is_not_the_reading_here: A record of two settings has no meaningful entry-step floor -- the median step of one entry is taken over the settings the record holds, and two of them are the ends of the table. And the low rotor's own run floor is 0.79 octaves, because one partial of four disagreed in two of its takes. Neither is what this run is read on. What it is read on is the difference between two takes of one byte, which is a quantity both takes' own scatter is inside: the two stand a fifth of an octave apart on the low rotor and the model, which never saw them, says so to four thousandths.

what_the_write_timing_took.what: `rests_at_hz` is a fitted number and rests_at_hz is where the rotor was when the write arrived, not a property of the byte. `short_by_hz` is not: it is the same on both types that carry this block and under every state either was put in.
what_the_write_timing_took.measured_by: One type, one byte, one value, three counts of how many bytes the run wrote before it. At value 12: 0.5934 Hz after two, 0.5472 after three, 0.4042 after thirteen. The multi that carries the same block returns 0.4042 after three and 0.4043 after nineteen, so this is a difference inside one type rather than between two.
what_the_write_timing_took.what_it_costs:
The bottom of the byte, and nothing above it. `rests_at_hz` is one of the model's two fitted numbers and it is not a property of the byte: on one type, at one value, it returns 0.5934 Hz after two bytes are written, 0.5472 after three and 0.4042 after thirteen. The other fitted number, `short_by_hz`, survives every state asked on two types -- 0.244 to 0.246 Hz from value 16 to 127 -- and so do the table and the direction argument, which are read where nothing is in transit.

What would restore the bottom is not a longer or finer run. It is a record that states when the write arrived, which no record in this archive does, and that is a change to how a run is written down.

And the low rotor's own run floor is 0.79 octaves, because one partial of four disagreed in two of its takes. Neither is what this run is read on. What it is read on is the difference between two takes of one byte, which is a quantity both takes' own scatter is inside: the two stand a fifth of an octave apart on the low rotor and the model, which never saw them, says so to four thousandths.

what_the_write_timing_took.what: `rests_at_hz` is a fitted number and rests_at_hz is where the rotor was when the write arrived, not a property of the byte. `short_by_hz` is not: it is the same on both types that carry this block and under every state either was put in.
what_the_write_timing_took.measured_by: One type, one byte, one value, three counts of how many bytes the run wrote before it. At value 12: 0.5934 Hz after two, 0.5472 after three, 0.4042 after thirteen. The multi that carries the same block returns 0.4042 after three and 0.4043 after nineteen, so this is a difference inside one type rather than between two.
what_the_write_timing_took.what_it_costs:
The bottom of the byte, and nothing above it. `rests_at_hz` is one of the model's two fitted numbers and it is not a property of the byte: on one type, at one value, it returns 0.5934 Hz after two bytes are written, 0.5472 after three and 0.4042 after thirteen. The other fitted number, `short_by_hz`, survives every state asked on two types -- 0.244 to 0.246 Hz from value 16 to 127 -- and so do the table and the direction argument, which are read where nothing is in transit.

What would restore the bottom is not a longer or finer run. It is a record that states when the write arrived, which no record in this archive does, and that is a change to how a run is written down.
